utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today we are Tuesday, 11th of December 2007. I would like to greet all the members of the Prosecution, the Defence teams. I would like to greet the accused, our witness as well, and all people who are assisting us in and around this courtroom. I will first hand the floor to the registrar for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One of the parties have submitted list of documents to be tendered through Witness BB. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number 745. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Tomorrow we will have a witness, we will not give his name because he is benefiting from protective measures, and he will be heard under 92 ter, the Prosecution will have 30 minutes to present the six documents which will be shown to the witness, and the Defence will have, in turn, two hours and I have to say that the accused Petkovic as well as Praljak will have each 30 minutes and the other Defence teams ten minutes, which brings us theoretically to a shorter hearing for that witness. Furthermore, as you may know, I am sitting in another trial as well and since in this other trial we are slightly delayed or we were slightly delayed today, tomorrow's hearing will not begin at 2.15 for this witness as usual but it will begin at 3.15. So this is what I wanted to say to the parties so the cross-examination of this witness is starting immediately. I do not know what is the order -- oh, I see that Ms. Nozica is on her feet. So I would like to wish her good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Ribicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have provided my set of documents to everybody. At this moment, the witness is also being provided with the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Professor Ribicic, I will advise you when to look at the documents, but please focus on my questions. I have noticed that you don't speak too fast so that should not be a problem. I just need to tell you that we both speak the same language. We have to make sure to make short pauses between my questions and your answers. Professor Ribicic, in your analysis and in your testimony, you have referred to the decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina of September 1993, which make null and void the decision on the establishment of the HZ HB dated 18/11/1991. I'm talking about document P 00476. Mr. Ribicic, are you familiar with the constitutional provisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina that regulate the constitutional position of the Constitutional Court and I'm concretely referring to the composition of the court, the way the judges are appointed, their mandate, the organisation of the court, the competency to start proceedings and the way decisions are made? We are talking about the Constitution dated 1974 based on which the decision in dispute was passed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I was preparing for my first appearance at the Tribunal, I had a look at the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then you obviously know that at the time when the decision in dispute was passed, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina had nine judges. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to read the book of rules of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I'm not sure whether at that time I read that. I'm sure that I have not read it recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In my binder, among the documents, I have that book of rules. I'm going to refer to some of its provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for my learned friend and the honourable Judges I would like to say that this book of rules and procedure have not been translated. I'm just going to quote some very short provisions and before I ask for the admission of this document, I will provide the Trial Chamber with a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ribicic, you will agree with me that it is absolutely necessary to establish whenever you examine a decision of the Constitutional Court whether the Constitutional Court complied with the composition of the court that is provided for by the Constitution in order to be able to tell whether a decision, if it had been passed contrary to the regulations, whether such decision may have legal effect, i.e., whether it can be then stated that this decision was passed contrary to those documents. Would that be only logical once -- at the moment when you are examining a decision?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it comes to the theoretical re-examination, then the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to look at the list [as interpreted] of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number U 46/92, which shows the entire procedure which was followed when this decision was passed?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is then logical that you did not have an occasion to see the record of the meeting of the Constitutional Court which took place on the 9th of July 1992, at which it was decided to launch the constitutional procedure to examine the constitutionality and legality of the decision on the aforementioned general documents. I have just been informed that there is a mistake in the transcript on page 4, line 14, it says a list instead of case. Thank you. So you did not have an occasion to see this record, did you?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It arises from the decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 14 September 1993 which makes null and void the decisions on the establishment of the HZ HB dated 18 November 1991 and the other eight decisions and decrees. It arises from this decision that the Constitutional Court started the procedures at their own initiative. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember and I controlled it last night because yesterday I made a mistake and to the Prosecutor's question, who insisted on asking me whether the government had started the proceedings before the Constitutional Court. I said yes, and that answer was wrong. The Constitutional Court did not make this decision based on somebody else's request. It was their own initiative and I apologise for making that mistake. Only the second decision that referred to the documents of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was passed after the procedure that was launched at the request of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Ribicic, that's why I'm asking you this. Then we can also confirm something else. Yesterday you said that in the first decision, we are talking about the decision that was passed on the 14th of September 1993, the Judges were evoking the opinion of the government which does not exist in the first decision. You have made the same mistake; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was in 1992, not in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well then. I would now kindly ask you to look at the minutes of the meeting of the Constitutional Court which took place on 9 July 1992, the document number is 2D 00592. It is in my binder, the second document in my binder. Mr. Ribicic, here you see that this is an excerpt from the minutes from the Constitutional Court session held on 9 July 1992. At the end we see who took minutes. That was Nikolja Grbic [phoen], that may mean nothing to you but this is the name that is stated herein and here is also a list of the Judges who were present during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. The French booth was not on. Are you sleeping?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Five judges attended the meeting and you will agree with me, I believe, there were four Bosniaks, and one Serb. And Judge Pero Krijan sent his apologies according to this excerpt. He was the only judge of the Constitutional Court who hailed from the ranks of the Croatian people. This may be pretentious, but can you agree judging by the names and I believe you are also familiar with the names, that you know these people?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know personally just Dr. Kasim Trnka and Mr. Milicevic, but I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would kindly ask you to look at the second page of the minutes, line 2, of this decision, where it says, "These are the conclusions. It says that the decision on starting the procedure of this matter is sent to the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Croatian Democratic Union with a request to sends to the Court, and this is very important, if they have them the full texts of the disputed documents as well as their opinions should be sent immediately. Professor Ribicic, does it arise from the minutes of the meeting that the -- at the moment when the Constitutional Court passed this decision to start the proceedings to re-examine the constitutionality of the decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the other eight acts -- documents, did not have the text of the disputed decisions?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be concluded from this that it did not have at their disposal the texts which were official documents and that it was only familiar with the acts from other sources, from the press, maybe it was in possession of some photocopies or something like that. As much as I could see today and from the documents that we discussed yesterday, that Mr. Scott was referring to, it seems that the Constitutional Court requested from the Croatian Democratic Union the official documents, the body of those documents, so it's very hard for me to say at this moment how many documents the Constitutional Court had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will come to that what they actually had, but now I would ask to you look at document 2D 00591 which is the book of rules and procedure of the Constitutional Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, I know time is precious but perhaps it's happening to others as well. The translation is going extremely quickly and I think it's difficult to follow and I assume that's because the speakers are also speaking very, very quickly. I think it would assist everyone in the courtroom and certainly assist me if the translation would be a bit slower, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That would mean that the original speakers must be slower because the translation is normally not faster than the translated speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Judge Trechsel. That was the meaning of my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I was convinced that Mr. Ciril Ribicic and myself both speak slowly. I apologise. I only have 30 minutes or maybe a minute or so more, and when it comes to such serious questions this is very short; that's why I may be speaking fast. Sir, you have been able to locate the book of rules. Can we now look at Article 23 and 33. They are on the same page. I apologise, 23, 32 and 33. Mr. Ribicic, these are the rules that are almost identical to all the constitutional courts in the former Yugoslavia. It says in Article 23 that the Constitutional Court discusses and decides pursuant to a written submission, and it says, a submission has to contain the following. Under number 4, the text of the provisions, regulations or other general documents, the constitutionality or legality of which is being challenged. Article 32 says as follows: A proposal for the re-examination of constitutionality and legality has to contain the following: The name of the document or a general document and the indication of the provision that is in dispute as well as the name and the number of the Official Gazette in which this document was first published. Article 33 says that if the document in dispute has never been published in the Official Gazette, then it has to be provided in a certified copy in order to be able to become a subject of re-examination. Mr. Ribicic, this is something that is logical, a decision cannot be passed without a document or its copy?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do we agree that there was a discussion about documents that were of great interest for the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely. But not only of the Croatian people but all the other peoples and ethnic minorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I agree with you but you will see what my question is going to develop into so I insisted on this point because of that but would you agree with me that if the Constitutional Court discusses matters of national interest of only one of the constituent peoples, as designated by the Constitution, and if there is a judge elected to the Constitutional Court from the ranks of that people, that making a decision in his absence might constitute a violation of the national interests of that people?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question is difficult for me to answer. A violation or prejudice to the national interests, this is a concept that we will not find in the rules of procedure of the Constitutional Court, so this is not a violation of the procedure as it is stipulated by the constitution, the rules of procedure or in any other way so national interest is something that we could not find there among all the possible violations of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's why I'm not referring to the constitution. I'm not referring to the rules of procedure here but I'm asking you in the practice of the work of the Constitutional Court, would this be the usual practice? In the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are such provisions but is this something that should be taken into account when issues of this nature are being discussed?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All nine judges should be present when any decision is taken, particularly if we are talking about the merits, the substantive provisions. As for the current provisions, in peacetime the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a decision that was voted for only by Bosniaks, Bosniak judges, and those judges who were appointed by the international community. I actually was very critical of this practice in an article, in a paper that I wrote. This pertained to issues that were very important for all three constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sure that you know so much about that but now we have veered off from our topic, the topic of our cross-examination. I would be delighted to hear all that you could tell us about it but we are running short of time.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will just allow me --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that in peacetime it can happen that all the Judges representing one nation vote against this decision, yet the decision of the Constitutional Court remains valid and legally binding. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely. Because the required number of judges voted for that decision to be passed in accordance with the rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the minimum of five votes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. In this case file, 46/92, there is a handwritten record of this session so could we please look at 2D 00593? This is the third document in my binder. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can see the date is the 9th of July 1992, again we can see that Ms. Nikolja is again mentioned here as a clerk. She signed the typewritten minutes. What I want to point your attention to is the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, this document astonishes me. How were you able to get ahold of this document? In all jurisdictions, deliberations are secret. This is a deliberation, in fact. How were you able to get this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not the record of the debate. I obtained it when I examined the case file of the Constitutional Court. The case file that I referred to. And this is the record that was typewritten later. This is supposed to be the same record as the one that we have seen a minute ago, that would be Exhibit 2D 00592. It is interesting to note here that we have two records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not answering my question. You are a lawyer. You are bound by the deontology of lawyers. My question is very simple: How were you able to get hold of this document. It is a handwritten document of the 9th of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked that this case file be examined for the purpose of the Defence and I received a photocopy of the record. Now, as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who gave it to you? Who sent it to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The secretary of the Constitutional Court for the purpose of the Defence, and if necessary, witnesses may be called to confirm not only this record but other records that I will be showing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So Mr. Ribicic, we see a handwritten record here that was typed up later but the difference between this one and the previous one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me just a second, please, you are a member of a constitutional council. Is it usual that what constitutional judges say during their deliberations be communicated to the outside world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the practice. This is the custom, and sometimes there is even regulation or a provision preventing this from being disclosed, and the deliberations are secret before the Constitutional Court, many other courts and international courts and if anyone were to ask for such a record at the Constitutional Court of Slovenia, that person would not be able to obtain that even if there were an interest an intrinsic interest in reading this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ribicic, I think it is not controversial that we have a legal interest in that but this is not the record of the deliberations. This is the record of the procedure to -- whereby a decision was taken to re-examine the legality and constitutionality of the decision. It is obvious from this that only four judges took part in the debate. If you go through the record, you will see that there is nothing about what Mr. Kasim Trnka contributed. Can we agree?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we please look at the intervention by Mr. Latic, that's on page 1 in the Croatian version, and the first page in the English version, let me just read a part of it where he says, "Do they have decisions that we learned of from the press?" And this proves what you've just told us, that the Constitutional Court instituted proceedings to evaluate the constitutionality on the basis of press articles and reports. Could we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is very difficult for me to participate in this debate because I have to agree with what you've just said, that this is the part of the deliberations of the Court which should remain secret. So confidential. So I would not like to say anything about what we are not supposed to know at all. Especially not about views taken by particular judges. We have to limit ourselves to what was actually made public, and I personally cannot, and I don't think that we can, discuss this in this manner. It would be unprofessional, I posit. It would be unprofessional to discuss what the Judges said during their internal debate, particularly not on the basis of a handwritten document written by a third party. I think that I will have to recuse myself from this debate because I think that I would engage in unprofessional practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ribicic, let us set aside the minutes. Let me ask you a hypothetical question. So here comes the hypothetical question. If in this debate [French interpretation] participation of only four out of nine elected judges to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina [French interpretation] accordance with the rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again the French booth has a problem. I'm not getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I begin and then we can see?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So let me repeat, because some things were not interpreted. My question to you is: If really only four of the Judges took part in taking this decision, if, and we concluded that the Constitutional Court had nine judges, would then this decision be contrary to the rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. The Constitutional Court cannot take any decisions if less than five judges are present.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Likewise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, you were assuming that only four judges were present at that meeting because the desk officers or whoever wrote this does not -- does only refer to pronunciations by four. If you look at the excerpt from minutes you have five there. The fact that one judge does not take the floor in deliberations does not mean that he does not participate. On what do you base the assumption that only four judges participated?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am assuming on this on the difference between the two documents and now, as to whether there were four of them or five of them, that is why I asked the expert witness to give me an answer to a hypothetical question about whether a decision would be valid if only four of the Judges were present. Now, as to whether four or five of the Judges were present or not, we will deal that in our Defence case. In the 30 minutes that I have allotted for my cross-examination, I cannot explain to the Judges which judges were present there, the documents appointing them and so on, to confirm the arguments in my cross-examination. That is why I'm only asking the expert witness to confirm how decisions are made on the basis of this hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Professor Ribicic, do you agree also that if the Constitutional Court took its decision on the basis of a press article without having access to the full text of the decision, that this would constitute a violation of the rules of procedure of the Constitutional Court?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in peacetime, in normal circumstances, there would be nine judges there. That's for sure. And they would all have participated and they would have made the decision to launch the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ribicic, can the constitution be violated in this manner in wartime by saying, no, we don't need nine judges any more, five is enough, or is the constitution which stipulates that nine members of the Constitutional Court should be there and that decisions should be passed by a majority of votes, so is there a time, and is there a decision that is taken contrary to the provisions of the constitution, is it an illegal decision particularly if we are talking about these two questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, we see very well what you're getting at but your strategy would have been better received if you had given the Judges in the English version the translation of the Statute of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is now in B/C/S and I don't have it in English. If I had had it in English, I would have looked at the Articles very quickly but I cannot make that verification so I am handicapped in a certain way but independently of that, you may put your question. We understood you; we are judges. We don't need hours and hours to understand what you're getting at so please go ahead and ask the most important question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have asked my question. Let me repeat it for the third time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is the decision to institute the proceedings taken by four of the nine judges that were elected to the Court and on the basis of a press article, so not even a copy of the document that is being evaluated, would such a decision be contrary to the Constitution and the rules of procedure binding the Court?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise for interrupting. I'm not sure if we changed gears or not. The question that was just put to the witness was if the decision would institutes the proceedings, not the decision on the merits, I do believe if I'm not mistaken even in the United States Supreme Court, a minority of the Judges can decide which cases to hear and this is what says here if the decision to institute the proceedings taken by four of the nine judges, so that's not the same thing as a decision on the merits by how many judges, so I don't know if counsel meant to say that or -- that's why I stand up for perhaps some clarification would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It is not necessary. I said quite clearly that all the decisions taken by the Constitutional Court and we can look at Article 46 of the rules of procedure, where it says that the meetings of the constitutional -- the Constitutional Court shall meet as necessary and a session of the Constitutional Court can take place if attended by the majority of the Constitutional Court. So regardless of what the decision is going to be about, a majority of the Judges must be present.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Ribicic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you do not address the point made by Mr. Scott. Your first question was whether the majority voted for the decision. Now you are talking about whether the Court can sit when the majority are present. And those are two different things, and the difference may -- may, be of a decisive importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, I'm talking about the decision to institute proceedings and not decision on the merits. We haven't touched upon the decision on the merits. And let me add one more remark for the witness, or just read one more article of the rules of procedure, Article 52 for the transcript where it says in paragraph 2 decisions are made by a majority of the votes of all the members of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this is the only provision on how the vote is to be taken and there is no distinction between decisions to institute proceedings and decisions on the merits. Mr. Ribicic could you please give us your opinion?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got this decision of the Constitutional Court I asked myself what the situation was like regarding the vote, who was present, who voted for, who voted against, but I couldn't find the answer to those questions. I would like to note that the decision of the Constitutional Court published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this Tribunal cannot decide whether it was legal or constitutional or not. We can all have our opinions. They may be different. But there is no procedure whereby we could alter the fact that the Constitutional Court reached its decision, this decision was made public and it entered into force. At least I am not aware of any option that would be available in any European country to declare null and void such a decision in any way by proffering arguments that the Constitutional Court violated its own internal procedure, the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ribicic, I'm perfectly aware of that. I'm an attorney too. We cannot do that but we can ask ourselves whether at the time the decision was made in a legal manner or not. We are not now filing a motion to assess the legality. We just want to find out how this decision was taken, who took it and so on. So could we please move on? You didn't give me your answer to my question, but from what you've just told us, I can conclude that you don't want to enter into debate whether this was -- this decision was made illegally or not.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to agree with you that it is not illegal to take decisions but five judges must be present and that the majority of the votes is required for the decision to be taken. I think that this decision was not procedural; it was a substantive decision, so a majority of the votes on the whole panel is required, five votes, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you already used up approximately 30 minutes. Did you get some extra time from your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mrs. Alaburic has given me five minutes and I will be able to finish within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke, when Mr. Scott asked you about the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its opinion about this issue in Article on page 8 of this -- of your analysis which is document P 08060, in the Prosecutor's binder, I'm going to read that paragraph very briefly, you said that much before, immediately after the establishment of the HZ HB, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, pursuant to an opinion provided by the Ministry of Justice and Administration, concluded that these decisions of the HZ HB were illegitimate and against the law, contrary to the constitution and you quote probably from the newspaper Oslobodjenje and the interests of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and all of its people and citizens including obviously the Croatian people in the republic. Can we please look at that conclusion? I don't know whether you had ever seen it before. Let's look at that document which is 2D 00594. For that, let me ask you this. Your quote is based on a newspaper article; am I right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are, and I said it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have you found the document, 2D 00594? It is in the Cyrillic but that shouldn't be a problem because you are very well-versed in both of the alphabets. This is a record from the 104th session of the government which was held on 21 November 1991 which is in keeping with the first sentence of your conclusion in which you say that the government passed the decision far before the constitutional order Constitutional Court confirmed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down. The interpreters cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 3, which is item 2 of all the things that the government discussed and since there is no need for me to waste any more time on this, I don't want to go on reading the whole text. I'm just going to say that in the second paragraph, it says, as follows: "Starting from the aforementioned opinions as well as of the proposals and opinions put forth during the debate, the government has established that the decision on the establishment of Croatian Union of Herceg-Bosna, and the conclusion of the regional committee of the HDZ of Bosnian Posavina were not passed as part of the procedure which is envisaged for the establishment of any social or political association, nor do they contain provisions that might have any legal effect as institutions of the bodies of authorities because they don't contain the necessary elements." And finally the last sentence reads as this: "At the same time the government is of the opinion that these decisions were not even something that should have been a subject of discussion or should have been put on the agenda of a session of the government because this is a political organisation and political action." This was signed by the president of the government, Mr. Jure Pelivan. Can we conclude that this part in your expert analysis, when we compare it with the record of the government session is not correct because what you are saying here does not arise from the minutes of the session of the government?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my evaluation, I relied on what I could read in the newspaper Oslobodjenje and if you are trying to prove that this was incorrect we will then have to look at Oslobodjenje. I have to start by saying that something that was published in the Official Gazette or published elsewhere is true unless proven differently. The fact is that the government according to this minutes did not discuss this issue but before that they adopted a position which was very clear and clearly warned to the fact that the conclusions on the establishment of the Croatian Union of Herceg-Bosna could not be binding because they were not passed pursuant to the constitution that speaks about the establishment of the Association of Municipalities as a political association.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Ribicic, please, but the government did not say what you quoted in your analysis. I am not trying to prove you incorrect. I am just trying to prove that the source was incorrect. I'm not saying that your analysis was incorrect. I'm just saying that you relied on Oslobodjenje which did not convey the message from the government session. Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. With the caveat that at the session of the government, a position was taken towards that. Now, as to why this was not put on the agenda for debate is an explanation that points to the inconstitutionality of the establishment of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have read that and the Trial Chamber will certainly be able to assess the difference between your analysis and the source that you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions because I don't have more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might before counsel finishes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I have to ask for clarification and counsel could still assist, be allowed enough time to assist all of us, it's not clear to me in looking at this document in comparison to footnote 30 of Dr. Ribicic's report, and the doctor may want to refer to that specifically himself, to footnote 30, in which this is described as a decision, an opinion of the Ministry of Justice and Administration on the 20th of November, not a decision of the government and not on the 21st of November. I'm wondering if we are actually talking about the same document or not. Perhaps counsel can assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mrs. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... don't wish to use Mr. Karnavas's time. Could you please look page 8 in Croatian, 10 in English, of the professor's analysis where it says that before that -- immediately after the establishment of the HZ HB, the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina made a conclusion pursuant to an opinion. I was only dealing with the government. I was not dealing with any opinions provided or put forth by any of the ministries. And the rest I believe my learned friend can do later on in his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think we just clarified we in fact were not talking about the same document. One was talking about an opinion issued by the government, apparently by the following day by Mr. Jure Pelivan who was I think the Croat Prime Minister at the time as opposed to the opinion of the Ministry of Justice and Administration which was issued the day before. Therein lies --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me -- therein lies the importance of my question and I'm glad I did stand up and clarify it because we are not talking about -- they were not talking about the same two things, two separate documents, two separate [indiscernible], two different authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is redirect, Your Honour and it's eating up into my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It sounds to me, Professor that you relied on a newspaper as an original source in trying to draw a conclusion. Would that be correct, just pick up where we just left off?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct but only I would like to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're now in a courtroom. You will answer my questions yes or no. I asked you very specifically, you relied on a newspaper as an original source. The answer is yes. Thank you. Now, you and I know the newspapers cannot be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we are here in a proceeding that is quite different from that applies in your country. Now, when there is cross-examination, the lawyer can sometimes ask a fairly long question and the witness must answer by yes or no. That is the rule. Go ahead, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should note that he was cautioned by Judge May when he testified in Kordic because he tried to do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to what I said, you and I know that you can't trust what you reed in the newspapers. Isn't that a fact, because if we look at the newspapers, and we believe the newspapers, your only father has been characterised in many ways, including committing war crimes. Isn't that a fact? And the point is the newspapers are not reliable as original sources; isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact and I must say that what I had before me were the materials from the ministry and what I quoted in my analysis were materials of the Ministry of Justice which means that I relied on Oslobodjenje only when it came to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The answer is yes. Your father was accused of slaughtering Croats after World War II, that's an undisputed fact, that he was accused of that in the newspapers. I'm not suggesting that it's true or not. I don't know. But that's my whole point. That newspapers are not original sources. Especially if you're trying to do an academic analysis as you were requested by the Prosecution. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is fact and that's why I emphasised in the footnote that I have been quoting a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And nothing prevented you from going to the original sources. Nothing prevented you from going to the original sources. And let me give you a suggestion. For instance, calling or getting in a car and driving to Sarajevo and looking at those sources; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, if we are going to look -- and I'm going to get ahead of myself a little bit, if we look at your analysis and if we look at the introduction to your book which we'll get to, you even discuss in there that in preparation of your analysis, you, in fact, met with certain individuals whom you thought might be helpful in assisting you in providing a constitutional analysis, correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we are going to get there but first I want to clarify one point with Dr. Prlic. Let me introduce myself first of all. I'm Michael Karnavas and together with is Suzana Tomanovic. Together we represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic, in case you haven't noticed by now. Now, yesterday, there was a question posed to you by the President with respect to a reference that you had made in a previous case that -- where my client's name, Dr. Jadranko Prlic was mentioned and you were asked concretely yesterday whether you had consulted him as one of the people or whether he had contacted you in preparation for your report, and you indicated that you could not be certain because after all, seven years had gone by. Since then I spoke with Dr. Jadranko Prlic and this is what he tells me - and perhaps you can assist, if this refreshes your memory - that approximately on August 2005, there was a conference -- in August 2000 there was a five-day conference organised by the Open Society Fund for Croatia, it was in apparently you were there and Dr. Prlic was there and you ran into each other. Might that be the encounter that you were thinking of when the question was posed to you by the President?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that what you're saying is correct, that Dr. Tomac organised the meeting which lasted maybe 60 minutes or so, and that at that meeting we discussed my questions that I had put about the preparations of this constitutional legal analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The point that I'm trying to drive home is that this was in August 2000, you prepared your report in 1999, isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you ran into Dr. Prlic after you had prepared your report after you had consulted those individuals who you thought, who you thought, might be important, might have vital and objective information to assist you in your analysis, your constitutional analysis as opposed to a political or historical analysis, correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, and that was after you testified as well?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that this is an error in the dates. This must have been before my -- what I'm saying is that my meeting with Dr. Prlic certainly did not take place after my first appearance here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we have a transcript of your appearance, it was on the 15th and 16th of February 2005. Assuming and we can check this out -- 2000, I'm sorry, 2000, and assuming the conference took place in August 2000, logic would have it that the conference was after your testimony and after, as you indicated, seven years passed so... But in any event I don't want to dwell on this point. All right. Well, okay. Very well?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I insist on my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was hoping to get one but that's fine, Your Honour, I'll move on. I don't have time. Yesterday you were asked a question at the end concerning the book that you wrote and as I understand it the book essentially is nothing more than your expertise that you prepared for the Kordic case. Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The book contains other things also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the testimony, the book also contains some other documents, also the transcript, there is also an introduction and the preface of the then-president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... title "Genesis of a Fallacy" and you made a point of telling us that that was a title chosen by the editors and then you supplemented that by also saying that the cover page was also supplemented and I thought that that was rather odd because and it was almost as if you were reading my mind, because the cover page and I'm showing it to the Court here, it has a cevapi on it and one would think, at least, if they came from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this was sort of a pejorative way of representing those from Bosnia-Herzegovina, someone coming from say a more sophisticated climate such as you coming from Slovenia. Might that be perceived as that, as I'm characterising it and might that be the reason why yesterday you volunteered that this was something that was chosen by someone else and not you?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from the book who was it who chose that. The name of the agency is Boze Sacove [phoen]. That's the page that they choose but cevapcici is not the important part of the cover page. The important part is the way the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina is represented in the centre of that cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is a word that you and the witness have used to describe the cover which apparently was not understood because you do not find it in the transcript. Perhaps you could be so kind as Mr. Karnavas and let us have a close look at the cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, and I will assist later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I assume that everybody in this courtroom had had a cevapi at one time or another. I highly recommend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event, I want to look at now at 1D 02036, 2036. And this is an unofficial translation of the introduction to your book, "Genesis of a Fallacy." I just wanted to cover some quick points. You could call this sort of a housekeeping matters for the next -- for the rest of the session before we go into the documents. Now, if you have it, I just want to point out a couple of things. On page 3, you talk about how you were asked to do this analysis and then towards the middle of the second paragraph, you say: "I thought that a critique of activities of Herceg-Bosna should be written (in Croatian) by someone who has always been a firm opponent of Greater Serbia unitary aspirations and to whom much credit goes for the independence of his state and development of its amicable relations with neighbouring Croatia." And then you talk about your reasons for testifying. My question is what does being critical or being a firm opponent of Greater Serbia and its unitary aspirations have anything to do with providing an objective analysis on a constitutional issue? Would you agree with me one has nothing to do with the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies to counsel, Your Honour, we don't have a copy of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. You should have copies of all the exhibits. We provided them well in advance. I apologise to the Prosecution, and I'm glad that -- next time I invite Mr. Scott to interrupt earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's okay. It's on page 3, counsel, it's on the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On your page it would be 19, sir, this is the original version. But in any event, going back, would you agree with me that being a firm opponent of Greater Serbia, Greater Serbia's unitary aspirations, I suspect what you mean unitary aspiration is one person-one vote, I think that's what you're driving at, but what does that have to do with you as a constitutional expert being -- providing an objective analysis? Would you agree that one has nothing to do with the other? It calls for a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on to page 4, page 4 of this document, again, staying with the same document, this is your introduction, you say in the first paragraph: "Due to the sensitivity of the matter, I decided that I would not write a single sentence in my report based merely on a priori viewpoint or even prejudice and preconception about Herceg-Bosna, but only based on reliable documents and information gained from authentic witnesses and experts." This would be on page 20 of your document, but I'm sure since you read English -- so it seems to me that at least here, it somewhat contradicts what we just covered earlier that you were relying on a newspaper and not on an authentic -- or reliable documents. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that I took hold of all the legal documents that were passed by the bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which means I did not base my analysis on any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- basis, but I first read everything I could find in those documents and this is exactly the explanation that I provide in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then you go on to say in the very same paragraph that you took a look at, and this is what I found to be rather shocking, the -- though perhaps not as surprising as it should have been -- that as part of your analysis you also looked at the expert report prepared by another OTP expert; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Dr. Zoran Pajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it you read that before you wrote your own analysis. In other words, you didn't write your analysis and then say, okay, now I can look at somebody else's, perhaps compare and contrast. This was part of what you read and at least it was in your subconscious as you were analysing the other documents and writing your reports in preparation to present your report and testify on behalf of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After such a long time, it is very difficult to answer that, but I'm sure that if I had thought that his analysis took in account everything that should have been taken into account, I would not have made my own analysis, I would have rather told the Prosecutor to use that. I would not have suggested them to commission a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir I'm just merely trying to get you to verify what you've stated. You can explain on redirect if there is such a -- if we get to that stage. Now, if we get to the next -- further down, the third paragraph, you say: "I soon found out that the opinion one makes based on the normative material contradicted the testimonies on the activities of Herceg-Bosna. That is why I decided to consult experts and some politicians with whom I -- with whom -- I spoke based on 18 previous prepared questions." And then go on a little bit. My first question is those 18 prepared questions, we don't have, I assume and the explanation might be because when you moved offices or moved houses, somehow they got lost in the shuffle, correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually destroyed them. I actually had them destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had them destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like everything else that I had and I thought I would never have to use again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you destroy them before or after you testified in Kordic?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was a year ago, approximately a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A year ago, okay. Now, sir, I don't have it with me and I'm really shocked to hear this because when I got into this case in 2005, I wrote you a letter in English. You responded in Slovenian. I asked to you kindly use Croatian which I knew that you knew and I asked you for your notes and back then, you wrote to me - I can dig it up, we'll find it - you told me that the notes got lost during the move. So if you destroyed the notes as you're telling us now in 2006, which precedes 2007 by a year, it stands to follow that at the time that I was asking for the notes, you had the notes and you deliberately destroyed them thereafter, even though you knew by then that you were on the Prosecution list to testify in this particular court, in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is far from the truth. You asked me whether this was after my testimony seven years ago and my answer was yes, that was much later, because of the relocation. At that time when you wrote to me, I never intended to come here. You know very well that I allowed the Prosecutor's Office to use my analysis but that I asked them and my condition was that I wouldn't have to come here, and that was a proposal to the Trial Chamber from the Prosecutor's Office and I was convinced that that would never happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You answered the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at some point, Your Honour, I will be tendering that letter just to make sure that there is no confabulation on my part that I had made the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, going to, page 5, you say that -- you go on and then you talk about: "Unfortunately," this is on the first paragraph, "some of my legal analysis proved to be more or less suscipient labour when I ran into the secret decisions of a meeting of the HDZ high officials to say one thing publicly and to write in documents and then (that HDZ supports sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina) and to do a different thing in the secret annexing of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia." And then you said: "As I found out about such arrangements after I had finished the basic analysis of Herceg-Bosna legislation, it seemed to be at least partially too detailed, limited by normative approach, sometimes even naive." I don't know what that means, but then you go on to say on page 7, on page 7, at the -- first paragraph, middle of the paragraph, you say: "That transcript considerably influenced my final opinion on Herceg-Bosna and its mistakes although I did not forget to say in my expert report that such HDZ policy was never officially accepted as the policy of the Croatian state especially not of the Croatian parliament which assisted on the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted a decision to recognise it, et cetera." Now, it would seem to me, sir, that at least in your introduction, that you placed high premium on that particular transcript and the transcript that we are referring to is the one of 27 December 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it -- and I should have asked you this earlier -- yesterday were you asked a question by the Prosecutor about your testimony in the Kordic case, he asked you whether the -- the transcript seemed to be accurate and you indicated yes. But I wasn't clear whether you were actually adopting the answers that you had given at that time, both during direct examination and cross-examination. I suspect the answer to my question is yes, indeed, those answers remain as they were back then, true, accurate and complete; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course, I am sure in coming here you looked at your transcript, read it, to see what you had said, to make sure at least whatever you say here was consistent with what you said back then and also to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm sure it must have -- you must have noticed as I had noticed that on the very first question during cross-examination, it was pointed out to you - and I believe that was on the 15th of February 2000, it was pointed out to you that about the chronology of the events and that this particular meeting had occurred as I understand it three -- three months prior to the referendum question, correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And for the Court's convenience lest there be any -- any confusion on that, this can be found on pages -- on page 2.000 -- 14.224 and the exhibit number is 103555 [sic], the exchange actually starts a little bit earlier but the answer is on -- on line 25 of this particular page where it says, "You could put it that way." Now, I'm told that the number should be 10355. That's the exhibit number. Now, moving on, I want to go now very quickly to your report and just cover a couple of points quickly before we actually get into the documents. If we look at the very first page, we look at the footnote at the bottom, you have the -- footnote 1 is an extensive biography, and at the end you talk about in drafting of this -- the very last two paragraphs -- two sentences or maybe it's the last sentence: "In the drafting of his expert opinion on the issue in dispute, he, Ribicic, consulted with several professors from Ljubljana, Zagreb, Sarajevo. In the preparation of his expert opinion he relied on Narodni List, HZ RHB, 1992 to 1994," that's the Official Gazette, of course, "the testimony of Dr. Pajic, in the proceedings against Blaskic in The Hague, works on the theory of the state and constitutional law primarily from Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and other materials which are cited in the expert opinion. My question now, I guess we'll park here for a second, do you have a list of all the people that you actually consulted with, that you could provide us at this point in time, or has -- is memory fading with time?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Memories fade, so I don't have the list but I mentioned some of their names in my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it did you meet with Mesic, now President Mesic? Did you discuss this with him?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you look at his testimony by any chance in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, obviously, you talk about at one point because I found this rather interesting I'm going to move ahead a little bit on page -- on page 41 of your report, on the first -- the second paragraph, you say: "With respect to its relationship with the Republic of Croatia, the legal enactments of HZ HB do not provide sufficient evidence which would indicate its legal subordination to its neighbouring state. However, a constitutional analysis cannot confine itself to normative regulations but rather it must study the actual state of affairs, the implementation of the normative regulations and the actual relationships in real life." Now help me out here, Professor. In reading this, this last part especially, it seems to me what you're saying that we cannot just look at the laws and at least do a de jure analysis but you're saying we also need to do a de facto application and in order to do that de facto application we must look at a number of things in order to make sure that we have the application in context. Would that be correct? And this would be on page 32 of your version, page 41 in the English version. But am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, but I have to say that I meant not only the testimony and so on but also to the documents that I obtained here in The Hague, in particular the transcript of the HDZ leadership meeting in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to get to that but I just first before we break I just want you to help me out here. Since you were embarking on not just a de jure but de facto analysis, and forgive me if I say that this is more of a political, historical analysis than a pure legal expert analysis, that's my opinion, but did you consult with some of the players, as it were? For instance, did you meet with Mr. Akmadzic? And that calls for a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know who Mr. Akmadzic is and what his position is?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Am I to understand from that that did you not hear of Mr. Akmadzic, you did not hear what his role was?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. What about Franjo Boras? Do you know that name? Did you meet with him, do you know in what capacity he was involved in this process?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think his name is -- do you know his name off the top of you head?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... So you don't know him either?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. What about Andrijic who was with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, who was this, the name was not recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Jure Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These are all prominent figures that are in documents that are already before the Trial Chamber and more will be heard throughout the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now about what Mr. Andrijic, I believe his first name was Stjepo, and he was with the Central Bank -- a governor of the Central Bank and the reason I mention this, the reason I mention this is because you make, at some point, some sort of an analysis or some sort of -- you venture an opinion concerning the Croatian dinar and I'm wondering whether you ever went to Sarajevo or found out who the governor of the Central Bank was and to what extent the Central Bank was functioning if it was functioning at all, and what currency was being issued and circulated in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the various places, during the relevant period that were you asked to analyse the constitutionality of these documents?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I said that I consulted people, I referred primarily to professors of constitutional law, experts dealing with issues in constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you wrote to Kljuic, right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote to him and he wrote back to me. I met him for the first time after my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you wrote to him, he gave you some answers, you incorporated his thoughts into your analysis; right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thanked all of them for the information they gave me, but I told them that I would decide myself whether I would include any of that in my analysis and that I will not be referring --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I'm trying to show here is not what you relied on. What I'm trying to show here is that you as an expert supposedly trying to do an objective analysis, given your own admission that you want to look at the de facto situation, it would seem to me that if you wanted to be fair and helpful to the Trial Chamber, as opposed to perhaps assisting one party or the other, you should have looked at or consulted with all these people who were involved. So let me move on. Did you meet with anybody, for instance, with the -- within the executive authority that we -- that -- of the documents for instance that you've been referring to and I'll start off with Dr. Jadranko Prlic? Did you meet with him to ask him any questions or did you send him the 18 questions to get his take on what was going on? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where is the proof of that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it will be a bit more difficult to find proof but we could call witnesses, but I did not talk to any people about that after my testimony here in The Hague. It was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you -- did you -- did you speak with, for instance, Mr. Zubak, Kresimir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what positions he held at the time?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He held a high position. I saw that from the documents. That's why I know his name but now I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay. What about -- do you know which positions he held at this point in time? Can you recall which positions he held?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wouldn't like to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about Zoran Buntic? Do you know him? Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you ever run across his name?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether I did or did not. I cannot recall what his function may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't think that it was my task to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you contact anybody say from the Muslim government in Sarajevo, Silajdzic, Ganic, any of those folks?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you consult, for instance, any of the texts or seek out any of the international players that were involved in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan or the Owen-Stoltenberg plan or even those who were -- Cutileiro, Badinter, any of those, did you consult with them at all to get a flavour of what was happening at the international level?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this can take a long time. You can ask me another thousand questions of this kind but I have to say that I quote sources that I used. In this specific case, the answer is no, but let me cut this short by saying that in the footnotes and there are quite a few of them, I list my sources, the sources that I used and those that I didn't use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, would you agree with me -- and we will be taking a break and I think we will keep this as the last question for now -- would you agree with me that when reading your report, sir, it does not read like a legal expert analysis because if we look at the title of it, it says, "Constitutional legal analysis of the establishment and functioning of the Croatian community Republic of Herceg-Bosna" and where is the book with the cevapi on it? I don't have it here but -- well, I don't -- I can't read the -- I think it's -- you have a colourful name for that, but again you note that it's -- you say, "Constitutional legal analysis of the establishment and functioning of the Croatian community" -- so would you agree with me that when reading your particular analysis, sir, it does not read like a legal analysis but rather it has a great deal of political analysis and perhaps even historical analysis? Would you agree with me on that? And it's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask to you be fair to me and my book. You should not really speak about it in the way that you have now spoken about it. And I would like you to allow me to answer. Anyone who dealt with constitutional law knows that this is a special branch of the legal science where it is stressed that in addition to the normative aspects which are of course the most important for any legal analysis, that sociological political science and others aspects have to be take into account. In constitutional law itself, in its very notion, there is an element that makes it different from criminal law, civil law, so I would like to warn you that in the title of my analysis, it says "constitutional legal analysis," not "legal analysis," so you're completely wrong when you say that this is not a constitutional legal analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this begs one last question before we take that break. If we go to page 44 of your constitutional/legal analysis, and this is what caught me a little bit, you say in the bottom part of the first paragraph, I might have to read a little bit above it, you say, in this paragraph,. "Viewed in the light, the establishment of the HZ HB was no doubt to serve as a defence against aggression, but at the same time, it was an obvious signal that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would rely on the Republic of Croatia in the agreement with the SDS for that and not for the government -- and not on the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims or other proponents of a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then you go on to say, this is what caught my attention, "This was boosted in part by a political segment of the international community which was fueled by a desire to prevent the emergence of a strong Muslim state as well as numerous demarcation plans of the international community which were (erroneously?) interrupted to mean acceptance of the partitioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that, is as the nation envisaging grouping in its ethnically homogeneous parts." So my question -- I asked myself how is this a constitutional legal analysis? And where do you base this - and it may be true, I know that there are all sorts of issues out there talking about the clash of civilisations and how we cannot have in Europe a Muslim state, even if it's within a state, and I'm sure you would agree that these were discussions, but how does this fit in and where is the basis and how -- what does this have to do with making a pure constitutional legal analysis of the documents? Because the Prosecution has asked you to do -- do that, at least in part, hoping that it would support their thesis of what the HZ HB or HR HB was all about. Could we have your comment on that because I want to be fair to you. Then we can take our break. Please keep it short. We'll have three minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely can do so. I first analysed the acts of Herceg-Bosna, and this analysis showed that this was a community that wanted to become an independent body politic or state, but other documents that you quoted and that I used, in particular the minutes, the transcript of the meeting of the HDZ leadership, showed that to a large extent, a political decision was made in advance and that the establishment of Herceg-Bosna was used in order to create a foundation for the annexation of that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the neighbouring Croatia. This is what I meant, and this is what Franjo Tudjman says quite explicitly in this transcript when he says that if this road is not taken, the international community will, through Milosevic and Serbia, prevent the creation of a new Muslim state in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it was Tudjman who didn't want the Muslim state. Is that what you're trying to tell us? Or was it the international community that doesn't want the Muslim state? Who doesn't want the emergence of a Muslim state in Western Europe? That's what I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tudjman invokes that and he says that the international community, in particular the United States of America, do not want such a state, and that they would try and prevent that through Milosevic, unless Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, just one last question, you say Tudjman but here you say, "This was boosted in part by the political segment of the international community which was fueled by a desire to prevent the emergence of a state -- of a strong Muslim state." I don't see a footnote to Tudjman. What I see here is some speculative analysis or some political analysis, maybe from other texts, but this is the international community, not based on what Tudjman's belief is of the international community but what you believe the international community is trying to prevent. Isn't that correct? And it's a yes or no and then we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, so that's your analysis, not anybody else's analysis.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes, but it is based --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
