utterances.text: Well, I don't see a footnote anywhere. As an academic, as a professor you know you have to footnote your sources. Thank you, we'll take the break, Your Honour, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. With regard to the time, I was told that you used up 47 minutes so I imagine that other counsels must have given you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, you did indicate it would be the smart thing for the rest of them to give the time to one person and although we already prearranged that, so I have the remainder of the time and I'm very grateful to my colleagues for providing time to us so we could do sort of a unified cross-examination. I hope I don't fail them in my attempts to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you talking about all of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a good thing. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hope my colleagues agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we go -- yesterday, I listened to a question that was posed by the President, Judge Antonetti, it's on page 32 of yesterday's transcript when he asked you the following question: "When the republic of Herceg-Bosna declared its independence and when it was not recognised as an independent state, since you are an expert in constitutional matters, can we make it -- can we make a parallel here with Taiwan, for instance? And then you indicated, as regards Herceg-Bosna, once it became a republic of Herceg-Bosna, it defined itself - Bozidar, please - it defined itself as a state community, not a state. It was done at a time when it seemed realistically to expect that it would be a member state or constituent state of some kind of federal or confederal Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, first of all, I just want to make sure that we are clear on one thing: The Republic of Herceg-Bosna never declared its independence; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was struck by that because I assumed Judge Antonetti was baiting you, you know, and you didn't respond. And isn't it a fact also that it never asked to be recognised internationally as such?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, it seemed to me, going back to the -- your analysis, that you said that you placed a great deal of premium on that one particular presidential transcript, and that was of 27 December 1991 and at some point you opine that the 30 municipalities that made up of the -- Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, this is on page 33 and onwards, you say that they had some sort of aspiration or was based on their aspiration to reenact or recreate or re-establish the Banovina. I'm paraphrasing but is that more or less part of your thesis? And you ground that in the fact that the Banovina is mentioned in the preamble of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. The 30 municipalities covered the territory that was within the territory of the Banovina Hrvatska, of course together with the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you seem to indicate, and this is on page 35, line 2, this was from your testimony yesterday, Banovina Hrvatska, as it was styled, covered the very same territory of the 30 municipalities that were included in Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And then when you go back, you go down to lines 9 and 10 of yesterday's -- on the very same page on page 35 you say, "The selection of these 30 municipalities were obviously governed by a certain historical and programmatic considerations." That's what it says. I'm just reading from the transcript. You stand by that, do you not? Because then you go on, on lines 21, you say, "This is quite important. I posit because we can see that Banovina Hrvatska is mentioned in the preamble to the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia." And that you make some allusions to that as well in your analysis but this is from your testimony yesterday and when I look at that it seems to me that what you're saying is that there is some sort of a connection between the 30 municipalities and the Banovina Hrvatska and part of that is in light of the fact that we can find a reference to Banovina Hrvatska in the Croatian -- in the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said actually, the territory of Banovina Hrvatska is mentioned but it was much larger than the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So Banovina Hvratska included that territory, the territory of the 30 municipalities that went on to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So when I asked myself why those 30 municipalities, the answer could not be that Croats were in the majority there because we know that they were in some but were not in others, so I tried to find out what it was, and I came to realise that it corresponded quite closely to the territory that had been part of Banovina Hvratska in 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. And I'll leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide but it seems to me that this is speculative on your part because you say, "This is quite important, I posit." It seems to me that you are speculating, drawing some sort of a conclusion, as it were. Can we go -- can I -- do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Prosecution did draw some maps that show that. I saw those maps. And there is a high degree of correspondence in terms of territory between the 30 municipalities and the territory that was made part of Banovina Hrvatska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine but what I'm trying to get you, sir, to confirm or deny is the fact that you look at the reference to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and you say, Ha, it's in the preamble, therefore, those Herzegovinian Croats and from Central Bosnia, wherever they may be, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, they must have the Banovina in mind, hence the selection of these 30 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know -- no, no, please, I want to draw your attention to the fact that Dr. Tudjman spoke about that quite explicitly in -- at that meeting. It is written down in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- why it would be useful for that part to be joined to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Just for the record, Your Honours, we have 1D 02039. This is the document, unofficial translation of the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia. I don't know if it's -- it's the preamble, I'm sorry, the preamble to the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia and it does indeed make reference to -- at the very -- if you look at the page 1, if you look at the page -- if you look at page 1, and you see that there are these bullet points, the second-to-last, it says, "In the establishment of the Banovina Croatia in 1939, by which Croatian state identify [sic] was restored in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia," and then it goes on and talks about the next phase because if we look from the beginning and start from the 7th century onwards. And would it be fair to say, sir, that this preamble, the way it's at least laid out, lays out the sort of historical progression of the Republic of Croatia in its various phases throughout the centuries?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I want to -- since we are talking about the Banovina perhaps we can look at a map and go through some documents because then -- and please tell us whether this confirms or denies what you were able to see from the Prosecution. And incidentally before I ask you a single question, may I ask do you have a list of the documents that were provided to you by the Prosecution? And I assumed when they did provide the documents to you, along with the six or seven questions, as you've indicated yesterday that you were asked to sort of answer, did you also ask for any other documents in the process? So, number 1, do you have the list of documents that were provided to you? 2, did you in addition ask for any other documents?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that list in front of me. I did see it at one point. And I did ask for some other documents to be sought, documents that pertained to the decisions of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now since were you also interested in context and you wanted to see how things were done in practice, I assumed you also looked at other places as well to see perhaps what was happening in Tuzla, Jablanica, other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to see what was going on, perhaps make a compare and contrast. And it's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now if we can go through --?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The first document, Your Honours, is 1D 01736. We have a map -- we have a map. It's on the ELMO, Your Honours, and you might see on the -- on the -- I guess it would be the left side, you'll see the colours and it's sort of a -- it's -- it's low-budget, but I think it serves the purpose and I'm going to go chronologically. If we look at 1D 01736, this particular document, this is a decision and we don't have -- I must confess to the Trial Chamber, we don't have an original decision that establishes the Bosanska Posavina as it relates over here, but here we see that Orasje municipality shall join the Croatian Community in Bosanska Posavina in addition to Orasje Municipality which includes seven other municipalities, Bosanski Brod, Deventa, Odzak, Modrica, Bosanski Samac, Gradacac, whatever -- and Brcko. We can all see it. I apologise to the interpreters and everyone about my pronunciation. Now, were you aware of this particular decision and were you aware that at least the Bosanska Posavina was established prior to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I did not focus on the position and the creation and the operation of that community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that this was -- this was formed in June 1991? The Bosanska Posavina? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that I did not really deal with that so I don't know about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you -- were you aware that there was such a thing as a Bosanska Posavina?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were you aware that these municipalities -- were you aware of this particular decision? Was that provided to you by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You think the decision on the expansion to include some other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. This one.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Look at the next document. This is 81, I guess it's -- P 00081. This is dated 18 November 1991. This is the first decision -- if we could leave -- if we could just leave it on the ELMO, please, the gentleman does have the document and if we could look at this document and also in conjunction with this, we look at P 0078, these are the two decisions in chronological order but essentially if we look at the map that's on the ELMO, we see this light green area or yellow that covers those particular municipalities that are mentioned in Articles -- Article 2 of document 81, and 78, correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then if we look at document 1D 01924, if you have it, and if we look on a map, you see there is sort of an orange colour, it covers -- it says here in the decision, dated 1 June 1992, "The HVO, Croatian Defence Council of the municipalities of Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj and Teslic based in Zepce are hereby entrusted -- are hereby entrusted with the defence of Maglaj municipality." Now, Maglaj municipality was I understand it was a predominantly Muslim municipality. Am I right on that? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is sure that there was no Croatian majority there, in light of the location of this municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And we can see that on the map. We can see those areas. And if we were to go on for instance if we could now go off the ELMO and on to e-court perhaps we can look and just focus just for a second on the presidents of the municipal Crisis Staff, perhaps you could tell us if you notice whether the names may reveal the national origin of these individuals, recognising that one cannot always rely on the names.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that we see some Muslim names on this, now Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, it's 1D 01261, and go back to the map, and go back to the map, this is from the municipality of Olovo. utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Next document is P 00741, and this deals with - you will notice, Your Honours, that we I guess we are running out of colours at this point and we tried to you'll see some lines on it, it's red with some lines on it - excerpts from the record of the Second General Assembly of the BH HDZ held on November 14, 1992 in Mostar, and I draw everyone's attention, including yours, sir, to page 5 at least in the English version, page 5 in the English version. He suggested that the Croats of Zenica form a Croatian municipality which would join the HZ Herceg-Bosna." Then if we go on to the following page, number 6, and we look at paragraph 10, Your Honours, and sir, "Tomislav" - I need some help - "Oberdan [phoen], Sarajevo," and at the very last line it says Sarajevo -- "HVO in Sarajevo be officially empowered to work and operate." And from this document it would appear that you have HVO in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at number -- number 14, but before we go to number 14, we can look at number 13 just to -- because we mentioned this name earlier, we see Mile Akmadzic, the Prime Minister of BH, Prime Minister -- I'm sorry, the -- so he would be the president of the government I'm told in the original language, they have it here as Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is -- do you recognise this name now that you see it in writing, Mile Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's why I asked you whether you had contacted him because he had been in -- involved in the activities. Now if we look at paragraph number 14: "Franjo Bratic, Usora, promised to unite Usora, a new Croatian municipality with the HZ Herceg-Bosna." And if we look at the -- at the map, you can see that it's again it's -- it's Usora. Do you know where that is, sir? I'm told that it's right by Doboj. You've heard of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see it over there and we have pencilled it in I should note for the Trial Chamber that this is a rough approximation based on Ms. Tomanovic's understanding of the area since she hails from there. Okay, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, excuse me, I'm a bit lost, are you quoting and referring to P 00741?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It has several paragraphs, I was on page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because we are a bit switching from pages to numbers. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm terribly -- I apologise. If I could just recap very quickly I first referred to paragraph number 7 on page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's okay. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 6, it was 10 and 14. Okay, again my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on -- were you aware of this particular -- this particular document, was this shown to you by any chance --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I trust the fact that it's a P number has not been lost on the Trial Chamber's attention. Now, the next document is 1D 01981, these are minutes from a joint meeting of the HVO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One quick question to the witness. The document that Mr. Karnavas just evoked with the various names and dates, 13th, 8th, 10th, it's an important document, right? Had you not seen it when you were preparing yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the document that I have on the screen before me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 741. Did you not read it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Since the comment was directed at the Prosecution by Mr. Karnavas which I don't think is necessary. I don't think we need counsel's comment during the questioning of witnesses, but since it was done, and since the question has been asked, there would be no reason to show these documents to the witness because none of these other areas are part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. They are completely separate items, have nothing to do with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which is the question that this expert was asked to address, specifically the operation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So while this is an interesting geography lesson this afternoon, it has nothing to do with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it specifically goes to what the gentleman has opined and I don't want to get into a lengthy debate. In any event my reference to the Prosecution, I understand I touched a nerve but the point was this, if you're asking -- if you're asking an expert to do an analysis and you have all sorts of documents that might assist the expert - since he is the expert; otherwise you would do it yourself - why not give him what documents you have and let the expert figure it out, as opposed to having the expert referred to newspaper articles to try to figure out what a Constitutional Court might have said. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas wants to continue arguing, Your Honour, then the Prosecution will once again respond. They weren't -- number one they weren't provided to the witness because they were, 1, irrelevant, completely irrelevant. Number 2, excuse me, I'm going to -- the argument was made, I'm going to respond, Your Honour. Number 2, the point should be made, this expert could look at any documents he wanted to. He's an expert in constitutional law. He comes from the former Yugoslavia. And I want to make it very clear that nothing he said or did was restricted to materials provided by the Prosecution. Dr. Ribicic could look at any materials that he chose to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I agree totally. If the prosecutor didn't provide it to him, because maybe they didn't think it was necessary, the gentleman who was the expert should have sought them out. He makes my point. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Calm down, Mr. Scott, calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to those comments. Now, stop it. Your Honour, take control of these proceedings and stop this running commentary by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had I known --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ask questions of the witness -- I have a thick skin but if counsel is going to stand up and continually make comments on the Prosecution, then I'm going to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very, well. I raised this question. I was astonished myself that the witness had not looked at this document. The Prosecution explained that they did not deem it important to show it to him so let's move on, please. Let's not waste 100 years on this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 019 -- 1981. This is a minute -- minutes from a joint meeting of the HVO of Banovici, Lukavac, Tuzla, Lukavac, Tuzla and Zivinice held on 15 December 1992, and this is a draft decision to establish the Croatian Community of Soli. And if we look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of this document? Was this provided to you or were you aware of this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we look at very quickly the next two documents, is 1D 0212013 [sic], this is a statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive government and administration in the area of the Croatian community in Soli?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, if you look at the transcript you see that the number must be wrong somehow here, it says 1D 0212013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have a statutory decision. I assume that you didn't see this document either.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we just -- just for the Court's convenience if we look at the very last page, on Article 19, the last page of this document, it says the seat of the HVO HZ Soli shall be in Tuzla. I thought this might be of some interest. And then of course we have the rules of procedure which in document 1D 02012 and I suspect that since the answers to my previous two questions with respect to whether you had seen these documents was no, the same would go for this particular document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... again because the issue was raised yesterday with respect to Official Gazettes and you indicated that municipalities did not have their own Official Gazettes but rather they would have to be published within the republican Official Gazette. If we could look at Article 4, just for the Court's convenience, "The custody and use of stamps shall be the responsibility of the secretary of the HVO HZ Soli in accordance with the decree on stamps." And then it says, "Official Gazette of the HZ HB," and it has the number. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to follow you that quickly. I have not found the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll move on just to -- for the sake of saving time. Now, you talked about looking at that one particular transcript which obviously had made an impression on you. Did you look at all -- did you read all of the available presidential transcripts back in 1999 when you were preparing your report or did you focus on that one and I dare say or suspect that it was probably brought to your attention by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor pointed those to me and I looked at everything that was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you look at all the presidential transcripts or did you look at some that were made available to you in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They weren't -- they weren't available to the Prosecution in 1999, Your Honour, or to anyone I know outside the President of Croatia's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas. Microphone for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If they were not available to anyone in 1999, not even to the Office of the Prosecution, how was it that you were able to get ahold of this particular document which belonged to the Republic of Croatia? How was it able -- how were you able to get your hands on it back in 1999? Because you seem to have been impeached by the Prosecutor here.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was provided this document by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I guess the Prosecution may be incorrect when he states that he didn't have those documents back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again do you want -- is the question directed at me or directed at the witness? I'm happy to answer. The document was provided by Stjepan Kljuic who was a participant in that meeting and had asked for a transcript of the meeting afterwards. And in the course of testifying in previous cases, Mr. Kljuic provided that one particular 27 December 1991 transcript to the Office of the Prosecutor. No other presidential transcripts were available, as far as I know, to anyone outside the Office of the President of the Republic of Croatia until sometime after January 2000. And I'm happy to provide that information to counsel, but whether this witness knows the history of the presidential transcripts and how the OTP came to have them, I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate and I'm very grateful to that particular answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There has been -- for sometime you've known that you were going to have to come here and testify, since at least 2000, the Prosecution has had numerous presidential transcripts at its disposal. It even has permission to use them. My question now is: Did the Prosecution ever provide to you after 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I need to make my question. He just can't stand up -- I know he's sitting there. I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Did the Prosecution provide you with all the other documents and say, "You know, Professor Ribicic, take a look at these other transcripts? Maybe or maybe not, you know, you will come to a different conclusion but at least since you're testifying IN this case, and this information was not available back then, now you should look at it to be fair to everyone, especially to the Trial Chamber who has to make a monumental decision at the end of trial."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now I will intervene, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Court may recall, the witness is here as a 92 bis witness based on a report that was prepared in 1999. The Prosecution in this case never asked him to prepare a new report, but he was tendered on the basis that his prior evidence in the Kordic case, both his transcript and his report, were tendered to the Court under 92 bis, that evidence specifically. And it was on that basis that the Chamber asked him to come and appear for cross-examination. At no time was a new report prepared or new information requested or given. He is testifying about a document prepared in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honour, I don't want to debate the point. I think if you're going to bring a witness here, especially an expert witness, they are going to present an expert report, it is fair that if new available information comes into play, that might assist the expert, in perhaps revising their report, that it should be made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hope you got the points, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the problem you're raising as to whether the witness was -- was cognizant with presidential transcripts when he drafted his report in 1999, isn't that the issue here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there is a double issue. One I'm trying to show that there is a sense of unfairness. They want to bring in somebody from 2000 with an incomplete report. They know that they have more information. And they can't say, well, gee. We didn't give this information to this gentleman and now it's unfair for us to confront him, In fact, I think it's unfair to their own witness to have him subjected to this line of questioning when they had information. I think they are duty bound, they are duty-bound to provide all of the information to the Trial Chamber and they could have done that through this gentleman and perhaps ask him to re-evaluate. I mean that's why on appeal, for instance, we have Rule I believe it's 115 that allows the Appeal Chamber to re-evaluate newly discovered evidence that wasn't available. What about due diligence? I mean, I can go on but I don't, I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when listening to you all here is the problem: You draft a report in 1999. Apparently you were not familiar with all the presidential transcripts because Croatia provided the contents therefore only afterwards to the OTP but apparently there was one document with which you were familiar because Mr. Kljuic had handed it over to the Prosecutor, that is one presidential transcript in 1999. You draft your report, then you testify in the Kordic case. Subsequently, after that testimony in the Kordic case, did OTP give you the presidential transcriptions that it had gotten in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, in response to further arguments by Mr. Karnavas, the Chamber will recall I hope that there are other witnesses and other experts in this case besides this one and all that material, all of this material, has been put before the Chamber. So for Mr. Karnavas to stand up and criticise the Prosecution for not providing this information to the Chamber is not only false but completely unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- I will move on, I just want to make sure that at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I will be moving that the report be excluded on the basis that it's incomplete. It's not dated. I mean, this is -- this is important to understand because he has anchored, he has anchored that report on that one transcript that we now know was surreptitiously brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's just not true. Don't make false statements, Mr. Karnavas. It's not based on one transcript. My gosh, there's over 100 footnotes, the Narodni List, the de jure, decrees, letters, communications, the decisions of the Constitutional Court. To stand up and say this is based on one presidential transcript is just false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. I think we ought to put an end to this battle which loses your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You seem to complain that the Prosecution brings a piece of evidence rather than another one, namely an old report rather than a new report, but now we have an old report and you will have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness on the basis of that, and there will be all the possibilities to bring other evidence and to show -- it doesn't help to complain because obviously this witness will not now say, I've read all the rest of it and it's all wrong and I'll change completely. We must perhaps also realistically take into account that to prepare such a report is a huge amount of work and I could imagine that the witness is not sitting at home just waiting for the next hearing and working on putting out reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have to go brick by brick and step by step to quote a very eloquent advocate of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're very right, Judge Trechsel. The only problem is my client is looking at a life sentence; that's my problem. That's a problem that eats at me every night and I need to point this out to the Trial Chamber that there is a sense of unfairness. That's what I'm trying to point out. It's not a matter of complaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's okay, but you have made the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, now we didn't get his answer. He indicated at one point -- it's on page 63, he had said but it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, 15 seconds. If I was doing the examination, this is what I'd say to the witness: You wrote in your report on page X such and such a thing. Let me now show you another document, the presidential transcript, that says something different. What do you say about that? That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to get there. I'm getting these interruptions from Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's my fault, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at one document now just very quickly, it's P 00498. It's a presidential transcript that's dated 17 September 1992. We already know the answer, that is that you haven't looked at it but if we focus on page 28, I just want to show you something. Actually it starts on page 27 and we'll see that it is a -- the -- okay, for you, sir, you will need to look at first the document, P 00498, and then -- and then at the upper right corner, you'll see some numbers, and you need to look for the numbers 01508797. It's on page 27 and we are going to be going to 28 in this particular document. This is where Jadranko Prlic is speaking and I just want to focus the Court's attention and the gentleman's attention on page 28 when he says: "The Croats, at least the soldiers in the Croatian Defence Council and the people who are involved, the organs of authority, have a clear political aim. It has been clear to me ever since I became involved in this and since I have been in this post. This aim is the forming and ordering of Bosnia-Herzegovina in accordance with the principles of the European Community, that is the constituting of Bosnia-Herzegovina through three national units." Were you aware that these were the words of Dr. Jadranko Prlic on 17 September 1992 at one of the meetings with -- were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we'll go to -- we are going to go through a series of documents, the title of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question that Mr. Karnavas should have asked you, if you had known this, that Prlic had officially said that he was in favour of a Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to the principles of the European Union and that Bosnia-Herzegovina could be made up through three national -- of three national entities, if you had known that, would that have changed anything to the way in which you drafted your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I did not write this report with regard to this case and Dr. Prlic's responsibility. It was written much earlier in 1999 and the transcript that I mentioned was taken by me as the basis to answer the question as to what was the motivation behind the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and at that meeting that I am talking about, Dr. Prlic was not there. He did not attend the meeting. But the position that was very clearly expressed there was about the motives for the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. There were people there who were in favour of a different option but they were in a minority. As for the subsequent transcript and my knowledge of them, they would not have any bearing on my opinion as to why the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established in the first place, something that I stated in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President because we have a witness here who no matter what he sees, and I suspect that's going to be throughout the case, is not going to change his opinion, incomplete report as it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to go through a series of documents, sir, and this has to do with context because you seem to have indicated you wanted to be fair, you wanted to make sure that your analysis was not only de jure but de facto as well. So let's look at a variety of documents and hopefully you might be able to assist us. First document is 1D 00894. This is from a text that has been used widely in this case and we will continue to use it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is a book by David Owen, "Balkan Odyssey," this is excerpts we are going to go through some of these. Did you ever meet with Mr. Owen who was part of the Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg negotiations. Did you ever meet with him?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now I know that his book is in Croatian; I don't know whether it's in Slovenian, but did you read it by any chance?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read it, I just read the excerpts that I found in the press or whatever was written in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you tend to rely on the press more than, say, these sorts of sources?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. If you look at the very first page or second page where it says chapter 2, "Establishing the conference," at the bottom of the -- of the first part of the paragraph -- page, it says, "The Netherlands had held the EC Presidency from the outbreak of the war in July until December 1991. And in consequence of my visit to The Hague, I discovered that on 13 July 1991, when the Slovenian and Croatian declarations of independence were just 18 days old, the Dutch government had suggested to the other EC member states that the option of agreed changes of some of the internal borders between the Yugoslav republics might be explored." Were you aware, sir, that the changing of the borders or the, at least, the thinking of that perhaps that might be one of the options, changing of the borders, was in the minds of the international negotiators? Were you aware of that at any point during this period of time or while you were doing your expertise?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So this was an option that at least those who were not home-grown, as it were, were looking at. These were independent internationalists that were trying to find a solution that would accommodate, perhaps appease, all the parties involved, right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you believe that the position that borders might be changed would serve to calm down the situation in this area, and that of course is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe -- I don't wish to do this to the translators but maybe I've been mistranslated. It's not what I think. What I'm trying to show you, sir, is that the changing of the borders was on the minds of the international negotiators as a potential option?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas, I think you are overstating a little. The foundation is a bit weak. What we have here is the Netherlands government suggests, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's not the negotiators, that's not the international community, especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Trechsel, I understand that. I posed a question in a general sense, and you will see through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Karnavas, you make a factual assumption. You state, Did you know that the negotiators did discuss. And we have no basis for the negotiators discussing. What we have here is one suggestion by one government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Judge Trechsel, but my whole point of the cross-examination, I don't wish to do a lecture on this, but I use that as a basis. We will see other documents. I wanted to know in general was he aware that this was something that was talked about because this is not the first instance, the only instance. I just want to know in general, perhaps it didn't come across that way, but I take the point. I don't want to be unfair to the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We go to the next -- now, if we go -- if we go -- stick with the-- stick with the -- further on it says: "The Presidency continues to feel that it is necessary to reconcile the various principles of the Helsinki Final Act and the Charter of Paris which may apply to the situation in Yugoslavia. It considers it especially important that selected applications of the principles be avoided. The principle of self-determination, example, cannot exclusively apply to the existing republics while being deemed inapplicable to national minorities within those republics." And then you -- then we have: "The following should be seen as a very tentative attempt on the part of the Presidency at structuring our discussion on the future of Yugoslavia with a view to developing a common position which may serve as guidance for possible troika involvement in the Yugoslav negotiating process." And then it lists four different approaches. "We seem to agree that it is not possible for Yugoslavia to continue to exist with its present constitutional structure intact. The joint declaration of the Brioni clearly states that a new situation has arisen in Yugoslavia. "2: It is equally difficult to imagine that Yugoslavia could peacefully dissolve into six independent republics within their present borders. Both Serbia and Serbian elements in the federal administration, not least the JNA, have made it plain that they will never tolerate the emergence of an independent Croatia with 11 per cent Serbs within its borders. "3: The loosely structured Yugoslavia constituting of six sovereign republics is not likely to assuage the Serbian concerns either. The higher the degree of sovereignty for Croatia, the greater the need for solid guarantees for the Serbian minority in Croatia. The looser the federal structure, the more difficult it will be to supply such guarantees. The foregoing seems to point in a direction of a voluntary redrawing of internal borders as a possible solution." So this is the Presidency. So, it's not just the Netherlands. And of course, there are other points that might be of interest, for instance if we go to the next page, he notes, in the first paragraph: "Incomprehensibly the proposal to redraw the republic's boundaries have been rejected by all 11 other EC countries." Then further down in that very same paragraph, he notes: "The refusal to make these borders negotiable greatly hampered the EC's attempt at crisis management." Then if we go to the next page, in the third paragraph, it says, at the sort of in the middle of the paragraph says: "There are indications that the Slovenian leadership passed on to President Milosevic an offer to deal, an offer for a deal under which Slovenia would stay neutral in the dispute between Serbs and Croats if it were allowed to secede from Yugoslavia." In any event, my point is -- and then if we go on to the next point, next -- next page, that will be page 36 at the very top of the page in English, this might be of interest. He says: "Milovan Djilas, who during the Partizan war was given by Tito the main responsibility for designing the administrative boundaries of the republics in autonomous provinces within post-war Yugoslavia, never made any secret of the fact that sometimes they were made quickly 'during a march' without the fullest consideration and were often arbitrary and driven by political expediency, and he confirmed to me personally that they were never intended to be international boundaries." Now, I just merely wish to point this out to -- and ask you the following question. Were you aware, at least, the internationals were thinking in those directions? That's all I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear to me that there were such ideas in the international community, as you say, either independent from all that or linked to what was happening on the ground, but you probably don't want to hear my opinion why those views were not accepted. It is clear to me that as far as the break-up or the division of Yugoslavia is concerned, that Milosevic asked that in that case, the borders should be redrawn and that wherever there are Serbs, that all those territories should be annexed to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. Unfortunately, we are not here to discuss all those issues. I just merely wish to point out that this is a topic that is discussed because we will see through other documents and throughout the course of this trial that these issues are being discussed by the internationals. Now, we go down to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before we leave the document and I didn't want to interrupt counsel's question or the witness's answer but I don't know how many times in the course of this trial the Prosecution has been criticised for taking something out of context, but since Mr. Karnavas has pointed our attention to page 36 and that line the Chamber might want to read the very next sentence, that in 1939 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's got redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- had given the Croatian nation control over the substantial parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Franjo Tudjman, never in their hearts accept the 19 -- I mean why couldn't we just read the next sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because, first of all, it's in the evidence. Second of all, unlike re-cross, which I usually get in my own jurisdiction, I don't get it here. He gets redirect. He's perfectly entitled to do that. The evidence is there for the Trial Chamber and now all he's doing is trying to obstruct. And do I object to these tactics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 3D 00281. This source is from a newspaper, Oslobodjenje. We can see it from footnote 1. 2 August 1991. And this is a text of a Serbian-Muslim agreement. Mohamed Filipovic, Radovan Karadzic. Do you know those gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never met them but I do know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of this particular agreement being published in the newspaper, since you seem to find newspapers as a source of information? Were you aware of this text of the Serbian-Muslim agreement?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I objected once already when you claimed that I base my views on what is published in the press, because in more than 200 footnotes, just a couple contained quotes to the press. So this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of this particular text of the Serbian-Muslim agreement --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next document, 1D 01538. Okay. This is a text, "Dividing Bosnia and struggling for its integrity." Were you aware of this particular text and in particular of the maps that are involved and are used in this particular text which seems to be -- the sources of which seem to be Muslim? And in particular if you look at endnote 35, covering maps number 15, 16 and 17 from Bosanski Pogledi, Sarajevo 25 June 1991? Were you aware of the existence of these particular maps referenced in endnote 35 --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not those particular maps but I did see quite a lot of those maps and proposals. As far as those particular maps are concerned, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you look -- would it surprise you -- well, do you know a gentleman by the name of Zulfikar Pasic. He's rather distinguished, lives in Sarajevo, has a foundation?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that these maps belonged to this particular gentleman? And again I want to stress the timing. I'm told he was the owner of the paper where these maps were published, and again, it's referenced in footnote 35. Was that brought to your attention during your research for this particular analysis?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00893. We've seen this document before in this Court. This deals with the European Community conference, it's 893, that's the number of the document. And if we look at the very top it says: "Editor's Note, the efforts of the European Community conference chaired by Lord Carrington were focused on a draft convention containing Articles dealing with," and then states, "general provisions, human rights and so on." And then at the very last sentence of the preamble it says -- of that section, it says, "The text of the draft convention as of November 1991 is reproduced below." Did you by any chance look at this particular document dealing with the treaty provisions of the convention of 4 November 1991? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not focus on that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at -- if I could focus everyone's attention -- on -- it would be 4(C), I believe, and that would be on page 16 on the English version, if you look at the upper left-hand corner, or if the ERN number for you, sir, I don't see there is an ERN number here. You don't have it. It says here: "In addition, areas in which persons belonging to a national or ethnic group form a majority shall enjoy a special status of autonomy, such a status will provide for, (A), the right to have and show the national emblems of that area," (B) is deleted, "(C), an educational system which respects the values and needs of that group; (D)(1), a legislative body; (2), an administrative structure including a regional police, police force, and; (3), a judiciary responsible for matters concerning the area which reflect the composition of the population of the area; (E), provisions for appropriate international monitoring." And I'll stop there. Were you aware of this particular treaty -- this particular draft?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I studied things that I quoted in my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I understand what you studied. I'm just asking you whether you looked at these documents because this is what some of the documents -- some of the negotiators were looking at. If we look at the next document, it's 1D 00394, and if we -- on the right-hand side of the top you'll see page 1265. We see this is a Conference of Yugoslavia Arbitration Commission, opinion number 4 on International Recognition of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the European Community and its member states. And there is an asterisk and it says, "Paris 11 January 1992," signed by R Badinter. Now I -- did you look at any of the documents that were generated by this particular gentleman, who was the head of a commission, Mr. Badinter?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did look at several documents, not only those that pertained to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the very last page under paragraph 4, just -- I'm just skipping through this because we have seen some of these documents in the past, it says: "In these circumstances, the arbitration committee is of the opinion that the will of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina to continue in SRBH as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established. This assessment could be reviewed if appropriate guarantees were provided by the republic applying for recognition possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens of SRBH without distinction carried out under international supervision." Were you aware that as of this particular date, with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was then titled, the commission did not deem it ready or appropriate to be declared an independent state? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of the reservations on the part of the international community vis-a-vis the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that you know that subsequent to that, there was a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since you met with or communicated with Mr. Kljuic, because now we know that he provided you with that one particular document -- and he at least responded to your 18 questions of which we don't have the questions of so we don't know exactly what you asked and what he said, but nonetheless, did Mr. Kljuic by any chance discuss with you the issues concerning the question itself, the referendum question?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at document P 00132, and this seems to be-- this is the original referendum question, at the bottom it says: "In favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, a state of equal citizens nationalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, Croats and members of other nationalities living in it." That was the original question. Now I want to focus before asking a question to the next document, if we could look at the next document which is P 09542, this is often referred to as the Livno question, and we see that it states: "Are you for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina state union of constitutive and sovereign nations, Croatian, Muslim and Serbian in their national areas [cantons]?" Were you aware, sir, that this was an alternative question that Mr. -- that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina wished to have at the referendum? Particularly because they, like the Slovenes in Yugoslavia, did not want to be under the yoke of a unitary state?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And a unitary state we understand it to be one person, one vote, and he who has the majority of the population would be in a position to at least suppress the vital national interests of the minorities, correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. But it was never mooted by Milosevic at all. His idea was a modern federation which would have been a step back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that but my whole point is I'm trying to make sure since we have a constitutional expert that we get the right answers, which is what the concept of a unitary state is and why some wanted it, that is, those who were in the majority and those in the minority were not interested in that kind of a government. If we look at the next document P 00118. Now we see this is February -- 12 February 1992 and we have here: "We have noticed that the reformulated referendum question is causing a fair amount of confusion among Croats in this area. Even we have difficulty in answering some frequently asked questions. We therefore request to urgently see somebody from the central committee who can provide additional explanations so that we can inform the public." Were you aware that at this point in time, there was this -- this issue prior to the -- to the referendum, that is, that there was confusion, and that there was concern on the part of the Croats, concern that the Muslim government or the SDA was pursuing a unitary government model?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but in the interests of accuracy, Mr. Karnavas keeps referring to the Croats as if they were a monolithic group. A part-- the Chamber, of course, has heard evidence that there was a split among the Croats in various parts of the country, there was the Kljuic faction at one time, there was the Boban faction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's fair enough for Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- to say this is the HD -- well, it's not a fair -- it's not fair, the question that was just put that the Croats, as if there was only one Croat view in Bosnia-Herzegovina and he can say it was the HDZ view, I won't object, if he says it was the -- it was the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- it was the position of the Boban faction of the HDZ, that would be an accurate statement but to say that all Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina took the same position is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document talks about the municipal board of the BH HDZ. It doesn't say anything about Boban, it doesn't say anything about Kljuic. That's what it says. It speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document P 09616, and this is an excerpt from the minutes. If we look at page 2. And it says here, under paragraph number 1: "Announcement of the Presidency of the HDZ BH, the text of the public announcement was adopted as follows: The assurances of the European Union expressed on previous occasions as well as during yesterday's talk at the conference of the European Union on Bosnia-Herzegovina indicate that the result of the forthcoming referendum will not prejudice the future constitutional system of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Likewise, fundamental principles ensuring the sovereignty of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in their national regions as well as in whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina contained in the decisions of the central board of HDZ of BH in Livno are not disputed. On the basis of the above, we call on the members of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to fulfil their duty and votes in the referendum. Now, were you aware that at least it took some assurances of the European Union to appease at least those within HDZ who were concerned about the question and were concerned about being in a unitary state? That it took the European Union to express, to calm them and to give them assurances that their national -- vital national interests would not be jeopardised if they voted yes for the -- in the referendum? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And incidentally, this date is 27 February 1992. This is one day before the referendum. Now, let's look at the next document, 1D 00398. If we flip to a few pages we'll see that this is a statement of principles of 18 March 1992 for new constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, before we get to that, if we look at the editor's note, it says: "The following statement of principles were agreed upon by the leadership of the three sides of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in March 1992. However, it was subsequently repudiated by the Bosnian Presidency." Now, sir, during your analysis, did you by any chance look at this particular document? And I mentioning this and I'm raising my voice to highlight the fact that you have grounded, it would appear and stubbornly maintained that there was this particular vision or course of action based on one particular transcript and now here we are 18 March 1992 and were you aware of these negotiations and this statement of principles? Were you aware of it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of the contents. I knew of the discussions. But I have never seen this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it when you were writing your report, you knew that, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or those representing them, among with those representing the Serbs and the Muslims, at one point in time, had signed on or had agreed to this statement of principles which called the three constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic, geographic, and other criteria? It goes on to say, "Bosnia-Herzegovina would continue to have its existing borders." No dilemma. "And neither the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina nor the governments of the constituent units will encourage or support claims to any part of its territory by neighbouring states. Number 3, sovereignty resides in the citizens of the Muslims, Serbs, Croat nations. And other nations and nationalities, who realise it through their civic participation in the constituent units and the central organ of the republic." And then it goes on to talk about the very -- how it would be governed and then talks about human rights, and you have the definition of the constituent units under (E): "A working group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic and other criteria." Defining the territory, geographical, other criteria. This is what is being written up as a statement of principles, and my question is: Did you take this into account when you were drafting your report, to say at least, yes, we had the presidential transcript, however, at least on March 18, 1992, these statement of principles was signed on and it talks about a new constitution? Did you factor this into your report?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took into account as much as I knew about the discussions, but I did not have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, would it be safe to say since you didn't have the document before you, it's not cited anywhere in your report? I mean, I didn't find it.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, when, yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to answer, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it in your report? I don't see -- you say -- you say that you knew of it. You say you didn't look at it. Where is it in your report that you make reference to this particular conference, this particular one? Show me the footnote. You're an academic. You are a law professor for 35 years. Frankly, you are a politician by occupation and by vocation, maybe, an academic and now a judge. But you've been a politician. But you, if you have been teaching for 35 years you should know that you need to cite. Where is it in your report? It's no where. Isn't that a fact? And I don't mean to be aggressive. I just want to move on.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer? If I may, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on to the next document, P00 --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked you whether you wanted me to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer the question put by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it in your report, yes or no? If so, where?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I can answer. I have to provide some more detail to my answer, if you will allow me I will answer, if not, I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer therefore by using a sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used a lot of things, I read a lot of things, and if I thought that I needed to quote something, I did that, and that is what you will find in over 200 of my footnotes. I did not quote anything else, and in addition to that, I also read other things, a lot of things that I referred to directly which allowed me to embark on the analysis. If I hadn't read all those things I would not have been able to do my analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: P 00339. I'm told that we might need a break. I don't know. If we need a break, we'll take a break. If not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will take a break, but I am looking at the clock. Mr. Scott, for the additional questions, how much time would you need for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to any additional questions. We were truncated, our cross-examinations. And this is outrageous if you can allow this gentleman to do redirect examination on top of giving him everything that he's wanted. We have Thursday, that's available. I strongly object. I have a lot of material. I don't see the basis. He wanted to bring him in statement only, statement and prior testimony, and his incomplete and outdated report. He's been allowed to do that. He's been given additional time to cross-examine. He's been jumping up and down like a jack in the box, sniping at my heels, and he's been making his redirect examination. He's been doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We understand your position but Mr. Scott may not require any redirect. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to say, Your Honour, I had been assuming that I wouldn't get any but I suppose if I could have five minutes it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if you need five minutes, it is 20 to 6, we will resume at 6.00 p.m. Mr. Karnavas if you can finish approximately around 10 to 7.00, Mr. Scott will have five minutes and then we can end our day that way. So you have approximately 50 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we to look at P 00339? 339. This is a Prosecution document dated July 21, 1992, "Agreement on friendship and cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of this particular agreement?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you were aware of this agreement while you were writing your report?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we just look at --

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just correct myself. I'm not sure that I had it when I was writing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at paragraph number 6, paragraph number 6, it says here: "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council will have its representatives in the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Were you aware, sir, that the HVO were an integral or was an integral part of the armed forces of BiH?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that that was how the agreement was written, but I believe that there was a desire for the situation to continue being like that if the agreement was to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. If we look at the next document -- okay, if we look at the civilian authorities, continuing on, that is, with the next paragraph: "Provisional civilian authorities established in wartime conditions, within the scope of the Croatian Defence Council will be made to conform as soon as possible with the constitutional-judicial system of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and talks pertaining to this matter will be initiated immediately in the spirit of the principle stated at point 1 of this agreement." I take it you were also aware of this part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01543. This is an annex and we see on the next page, on page 2, it's a joint communique issued on 1 November 1992, 1 November 1992, in talks between the President of the Republic of Croatia and the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it states that the Croatian president, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, met at Zagreb on Sunday, 1 November 1992. They reviewed the implementation of the friendship and cooperation agreement between the two countries, that's the one we just looked at, and if we go towards the bottom the last two paragraphs, it says: "The two parties have appointed their representatives in a joint committee for interstate and military cooperation which will start its work immediately." And then it says: "The two presidents support in principle the draft constitution of BH proposed by the Geneva conference on former Yugoslavia provided that it is -- that its final wording should safeguard legitimate interests and equality of Muslim and Croatian peoples in BH." Now, were you aware of this joint communique issued on 1 November 1992, where it would appear that the President of the Republic of Croatia and the President of the Presidency of BiH, one, are reviewing their friendship cooperation agreement, and two, in principle, are in agreement to the draft constitution of BH proposed by the Geneva conference? Were you aware of that at the time that you were drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that but I don't think I used the document but I'm aware of several attempts to re-establish friendship between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. This is Tudjman himself now sitting down with Alija Izetbegovic, right?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the next document very quickly, it's 1D 00814, this is a speech by Lord Owen. If we look at the bottom of the page it states that it was delivered in Geneva 16 December 1992. I want to focus your attention on paragraph 2: "One of our concerns is that the Bosnian and Herzegovinian government is sadly increasingly becoming representative only of the Muslim population. We are travelling tomorrow to Zagreb to meet with President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic in an attempt to bring together the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats into a more representative Presidency." Were you aware, sir, that as of December 16, 1992 -- well, let me rephrase it. Do you know whether Lord Owen in his speech -- okay -- and this is at a ministerial-level meeting of the steering committee of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, would you agree with his assessment that the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government was increasingly becoming representative only of one of the constituent nations and that is the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can note with pleasure that you asked me about contents. I agree with that and I agree with the attempts of the international community to re-establish normalcy in the relationship so that the representatives of both peoples would be able to act on friendly bases and allow for the Croats to be represented in the bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so as to be able to have a factual say in the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00892, this is the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. If you look at the bottom of the page it says signed in Geneva 30 January 1993 by Alija Izetbegovic, or

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic, R. Karadzic, M. Boban and as witnessed by C.R. Vance and D. Owen. First and foremost, were you, in preparing your report, did you consult, review, analyse and synthesise into your report aspects of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I just reviewed all that and I noted that one point when I noticed a link between the attempts on the part of the international community and the events in Herceg-Bosna. Otherwise, I restricted myself to my task at hand which was the constitutional and legal analysis. As for the international and military analysis, I left those to the others. I could not incorporate those into my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I go back to what you stated in your report, though, that one cannot do an analysis by looking merely de jure but also at de facto and would you agree with me at least, and I don't want to get into polemics, that if you have international negotiations and you have these three constituent nations, the parties, sitting around engaged in the negotiating process, would you agree with me that at least their efforts or lack thereof in engaging with the internationals in trying to find solutions, that that might be something that might be relevant in at least looking at the de facto part of your analysis, particularly since the issues are dealing with the drafting of a new constitution? Do you think that might be -- that would have been relevant? And it's a yes or no. And then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Now, if we look at this -- let's look at this document very briefly and see what the parties actually signed. If we look at page 250 on the right-hand side it's 250, it's it says, "Constitutional framework for Bosnia-Herzegovina."
